(CNN) -- South African Giniel De Villiers is the new leader of the Dakar Rally after he won Thursday's 12th special stage and Spaniard Carlos Sainz was forced to pull out following a dramatic crash. The stricken Volkswagen of Carlos Sainz after he careered down a ravine on stage 12 of the Dakar Rally. De Villiers, who was claiming his third stage triumph, brought his Volkswagen across the line in four hours, six minutes and 43 seconds -- over 16 minutes  ahead of team-mate Mark Miller, who lies second overall. American Robert Gordon (Hummer) was third on the stage, the same as his overall position. The route from Fiambala to La Rioja was reduced by 30 kilometers, leaving the special stage at 223km, as organizers accepted the Argentinian authorities' request to shorten it because of the archaeological discoveries made a month ago in the Fiambala region of Catamarca province. Two-time world rally champion Sainz, who was leading after six stage victories, had his dream of winning his first Dakar ended when, 79km into the stage, his Volkswagen crashed into a dry riverbed. His co-driver, Frenchman Michel Perin, suffered a shoulder injury and both had to be evacuated by helicopter for medical attention. Perin told PA Sport: "We had made a small mistake in the first part. We took the wrong direction at a Y crossing but it was not too bad because we did end up on the right trail. We were tailing Giniel De Villiers, who had started about 10 minutes after us, so it was still sort of okay. There was a hidden way-point indicated as 'danger' -- but it should have been indicated as 'extremely dangerous'. "The car behind us, Nani Roma's car, would have fallen in the same hole as we did if we had not been there already. I'm okay, I just have something broken in my arm, but I'm all right." De Villiers said: "It was really a tough stage. In places we would go around in circles for 15 minutes to find the right trail. It was very dangerous and the sand was really soft. "We stopped one time to deflate our tyres, then a second time in a huge canyon with tons of boulders. My co-driver Dirk von Zitzewitz had to get out of the car to find a way out. It was really a tough day." Miller added: "I can tell you that this was a very demanding stage. I cannot even imagine how the amateurs will make it to the finish today. It was not just difficult, navigation was almost impossible. "It was a long series of horror situations from start to finish. "These were the longest 200km in my life. The sun and the sand were so bright that I could not see anything." He added: "It's not good news to know that Carlos had to withdraw. He has an important place in the team." In the motorcycle class, title holder Cyril Despres (KTM) kept his hopes of winning his third crown alive after taking his third stage in a time of 3:57:37 to climb into second spot in the overall standings. However, Despres' Spanish team-mate Marc Coma did not make things easy for the Frenchman as he crossed the line 1:23 behind, to remain out in front with a 1:29:48 advantage. The 12th stage has been the most difficult since the rally began on January 3 in Buenos Aires, with competitiors struggling through sand dunes and rain in western Argentina. Sainz had held a commanding lead in the overall standings at the start of the day, having won six of 10 previous stages.

Sainz’s stricken Volkswagen careered down a ravine during stage 12 of the rally. De Villiers, claiming his third stage victory, brought his Volkswagen across the line in four hours, six minutes and 43 seconds—more than 16 minutes ahead of team-mate Mark Miller, who sits second overall. American Robert Gordon, driving a Hummer, finished third on the stage, matching his position in the overall standings.

The route from Fiambala to La Rioja was shortened by 30 kilometres, reducing the special stage to 223km, after organisers accepted a request from Argentinian authorities to alter the course because of archaeological discoveries made a month ago in the Fiambala region of Catamarca province.

Two-time world rally champion Sainz, who had been leading after six stage victories, saw his hopes of winning his first Dakar title come to an end when, 79km into the stage, his Volkswagen crashed into a dry riverbed. His co-driver, Frenchman Michel Perin, suffered a shoulder injury, and both men were evacuated by helicopter for medical attention.

Perin told PA Sport: “We had made a small mistake in the first part. We took the wrong direction at a Y crossing, but it was not too bad because we did end up on the right trail. We were tailing Giniel De Villiers, who had started about 10 minutes after us, so it was still sort of okay. There was a hidden waypoint indicated as ‘danger’—but it should have been indicated as ‘extremely dangerous’.

“The car behind us, Nani Roma’s car, would have fallen in the same hole as we did if we had not been there already. I’m okay, I just have something broken in my arm, but I’m all right.”

De Villiers said: “It was really a tough stage. In places we would go around in circles for 15 minutes to find the right trail. It was very dangerous, and the sand was really soft.

“We stopped one time to deflate our tyres, then a second time in a huge canyon with tons of boulders. My co-driver Dirk von Zitzewitz had to get out of the car to find a way out. It was really a tough day.”

Miller added: “I can tell you that this was a very demanding stage. I cannot even imagine how the amateurs will make it to the finish today. It was not just difficult; navigation was almost impossible.

“It was a long series of horror situations from start to finish.

“These were the longest 200km in my life. The sun and the sand were so bright that I could not see anything.”

He added: “It’s not good news to know that Carlos had to withdraw. He has an important place in the team.”

In the motorcycle class, title holder Cyril Despres of KTM kept alive his hopes of winning a third crown, taking his third stage victory in a time of 3:57:37 to climb into second place in the overall standings. **LA RIOJA, Argentina —** Giniel De Villiers moved into the overall lead of the Dakar Rally on Thursday after Volkswagen teammate Carlos Sainz crashed out of the race during a punishing Stage 12, dramatically reshaping the battle for victory with just days remaining.

The stage, running from **Fiambalá to La Rioja**, was expected to be one of the decisive tests of the rally, sending competitors through a rugged mix of dunes, rocky tracks, dry riverbeds and high-speed desert sections in northwestern Argentina. It proved decisive sooner than expected.

Sainz, who had led the car standings for much of the event, suffered a heavy crash during the special stage and was forced to retire. His co-driver, Michel Périn, was reported to have been injured in the incident, bringing an abrupt end to the Spaniard’s hopes of claiming a first Dakar title.

De Villiers, driving a Volkswagen Race Touareg, capitalized on the setback to take control of the overall classification.

“It was a very difficult day, and of course you never want to gain time because a teammate has had an accident,” De Villiers said after reaching La Rioja. “The important thing is that Carlos and Michel are being looked after. For us, the rally is not finished — there are still many kilometers to go.”

Sainz’s exit stunned the Volkswagen team, which had dominated the car category throughout the rally. The Spaniard had been one of the fastest and most consistent drivers in the field, but Stage 12’s treacherous terrain caught out even the rally’s most experienced competitors.

“We were pushing, but this stage was extremely dangerous in places,” Sainz said. “That is the Dakar. One moment everything is going well, and the next it is over.”

With Sainz gone, De Villiers inherited the top spot ahead of teammate Mark Miller, giving Volkswagen a strong one-two position in the overall standings. The South African, a former Dakar runner-up, now finds himself in prime position to secure a landmark victory — but he warned against complacency.

“You cannot think about winning yet,” De Villiers said. “The Dakar only ends at the finish. We have to stay focused, avoid mistakes and bring the car home.”

The route to La Rioja was shortened and modified in places due to difficult conditions, but it still delivered a brutal day for competitors. Thick sand, navigation traps and rough tracks caused delays across the field, with several crews losing time to punctures, mechanical problems and crashes.

In the motorcycle category, **Marc Coma** remained in firm control of the overall standings, continuing his measured ride toward another Dakar crown. The KTM rider avoided major trouble on Stage 12 and maintained a comfortable advantage over his closest rivals.

Cyril Despres, also on KTM, continued to push in the stage standings, but Coma’s consistency kept him at the head of the motorcycle race. David Frétigné remained among the leading contenders, holding a strong position in the overall classification as the rally moved closer to its finish.

“We had to be very careful today,” Coma said. “There were many places where you could lose everything. The goal is to manage the lead, but also to keep a good rhythm.”

With Sainz out and De Villiers now leading the cars, the Dakar Rally heads into its final stages with a new storyline: Volkswagen still appears in command, but the desert has already shown how quickly the race can change.

Robert Gordon remained the leading challenger outside the Volkswagen squad. The American, driving a Hummer, held third place overall after another consistent run, but he faced a sizeable gap to the leaders.

In the motorcycle class, Marc Coma continued to lead the overall standings. The Spaniard maintained a comfortable advantage despite pressure from his closest rivals, keeping control of the race as it moved toward its final stages.

Cyril Despres, one of Coma’s main competitors, remained among the prominent names in the bike category, while riders continued to battle difficult terrain and navigation challenges across the South American route.

With Sainz out, the car race has been reshaped dramatically. De Villiers now leads, Miller is close behind, and Gordon remains the best of the rest — but with several stages still to come, the Dakar Rally remains far from settled.
